s01: In chapter one, our question searched eleven chunks.
But what exactly is a chunk?
And who decides where one ends, and the next begins?
Here is the postmortem. Seven hundred and eleven characters long.
Where should we cut it? Cut in the wrong place, and the answer breaks.
s02: Search scores one whole piece at a time.
If that piece is a forty page manual, the one sentence you need is drowned out by everything around it.
And everything we retrieve goes into the prompt, so huge pieces waste tokens.
But cut too small, and a sentence loses the context that gives it meaning.
Chunking is choosing the right size of piece.
s03: First, how do we measure size?
This project counts characters. Letters, spaces, and punctuation.
Each chunk holds up to six hundred characters.
That is roughly one or two short paragraphs.
And each new chunk repeats up to one hundred characters from the end of the last one. We'll see why.
s04: The simplest way to cut is by a fixed count.
Say, every three hundred characters, no matter what.
Character three hundred lands right in the middle of the word, Ledger.
Worse, the sentence that explains why is split across two pieces.
Search for why the billing job failed, and each piece holds only half of the reason.
s05: So this project cuts smarter. It respects the writer's structure.
First, it splits the document at blank lines, into paragraphs.
Their lengths are forty seven, one hundred forty one, two hundred eight, one hundred two, and two hundred four characters.
s06: Now it packs paragraphs into a chunk, like filling a box, keeping a running total.
Add the next paragraph, plus two characters for the blank line between them. One hundred ninety.
Add the next. Five hundred and four.
The last paragraph would bring the total to seven hundred and ten. That is over six hundred.
So the box is closed. Chunk one is five hundred and four characters, and every sentence in it is whole.
s07: A fact near the edge of one chunk might depend on the sentence just before it.
So before starting chunk two, we look back at the last one hundred characters of chunk one.
Then we move forward to the start of the next full sentence.
That gives us: Hana Sato renewed the certificate.
That sentence is copied to the start of chunk two. Thirty four, plus two, plus two hundred four. Two hundred forty in total.
s08: Two more rules keep things clean.
If one paragraph is longer than six hundred characters, it is split at the spaces between words. Never inside a word.
And if the last chunk is tiny, barely more than the repeated overlap, it is dropped. So we never store a near duplicate.
s09: How much does the size matter? Let's run the real chunker on the postmortem, three ways.
At two hundred characters, we get four chunks. Sentences are split, and pieces start in the middle of a thought.
At six hundred, two chunks. Each one reads as a complete thought.
At two thousand, one chunk. The whole document. Precise search is gone.
There is no perfect number. It is a trade-off you measure with evals, in chapter ten.
s10: What happens if you change the chunk size later?
Every document stores a fingerprint of its content, called a hash.
If the fingerprint hasn't changed, ingesting it again is skipped.
This project writes the chunker's settings into a version label, and mixes that label into the fingerprint.
So when a developer changes the size and updates the label, every fingerprint changes, and every document is re-chunked instead of skipped.
s11: Where does chunking happen? Inside ingestion.
Parse the file into plain text. Then chunk it.
Each chunk is turned into a vector, added to the keyword index, and read for entities to build the graph.
Every search method in the coming chapters works on these chunks. That is why the cut matters.
